report.headline: About 15% of ALA koala remarks describe a sick, injured or dead koala, and 15 iNaturalist sightings never reached ALA.

insights.title: One in seven remarks describes a harmed koala
insights.essence: The keyword baseline labels 15.0% of 4,341 ALA koala remarks as describing a sick, injured or dead koala, with disease named 355 times and vehicle strike 181 times.
insights.detail: Of the ALA remarks judged to be about a koala, 577 state the animal was alive but unwell and 75 state it was dead, against 84 explicitly alive and healthy. Disease is the single most-named event (355 remarks), ahead of vehicle strike (181), rescue or care (89) and dog attack (17). For carers and council staff this is a sense of the mix of problems that make it into written records.
insights.caveat: These are keyword baseline (regular expression) labels, not ground truth, and no model classifier figures are in the pack; 3,605 of the 4,341 remarks have unknown condition, so the harm share counts only what observers chose to write down.

insights.title: Fifteen iNaturalist sightings never reached ALA
insights.essence: ALA holds 43 of iNaturalist's 58 NSW koala sightings (74.1%); 15 are missing, and 9 of those are openly licensed and unexplained by licence terms.
insights.detail: Six of the 15 gap records are all-rights-reserved, which accounts for 40.0% of the gap; the rest are cc-by-nc (7) or cc-by-nc-nd (2). No sightings sit in ALA's side of the shared namespace without an iNaturalist match. Anyone treating ALA as the single window onto NSW koala records should know a quarter of the iNaturalist stream is not visible there.
insights.caveat: The join is restricted to the iNaturalist observation identifier namespace, so it says nothing about overlap between ALA and iNaturalist records that carry no shared identifier.

insights.title: Nearly all the evidence is one dataset
insights.essence: NSW BioNet Atlas supplies 5,232 of ALA's 5,398 records (96.9%) and 3,946 of the 3,966 substantive remarks, so the whole picture rests on one feed.
insights.detail: The next largest contributors are the Australian Museum OZCAM feed (63 records, 1.2%, no substantive remarks) and iNaturalist Australia (45 records, 0.8%). BioNet also carries almost all the harm signal: 574 of 577 unwell remarks, 73 of 75 dead and all 181 vehicle strike mentions. Any change in BioNet's recording practice would move these numbers on its own.

insights.title: The two sources describe different kinds of sighting
insights.essence: 73.5% of ALA records carry a substantive remark (median 96 characters) against 24.1% of iNaturalist records (median 24 characters), and no iNaturalist remark names harm.
insights.detail: iNaturalist's 14 labelled koala remarks include 4 alive and healthy, 2 mentioning a joey and 1 mentioning rescue or care, with a 0.0% harm share under the keyword baseline. ALA's text is both far more plentiful and far longer. If you want written detail on condition and threats, ALA is where it sits; iNaturalist mainly adds the sighting itself.
insights.caveat: iNaturalist's text sample is 14 records, far too small for its 0.0% harm share to be read as an absence of harm events.

insights.title: Location precision differs sharply between the sources
insights.essence: Only 0.9% of ALA records are obscured beyond 10 km against 29.3% of iNaturalist's 58, and ALA flags 77.4% of records as having rounded coordinates.
insights.detail: Median coordinate uncertainty is 50 m for NSW BioNet Atlas, 220 m for iNaturalist and 1,000 m for the Australian Museum feed. Obscuring beyond 10 km is a deliberate privacy mechanism for a threatened species, not a data error, and the 9 matched sightings obscured in iNaturalist are also obscured in ALA. Field staff planning site visits should expect near-point accuracy from BioNet and a deliberate blur on much of the iNaturalist material.
insights.caveat: Flag shares describe how often a flag fires, not how far a coordinate is actually off; the pack gives no distance for rounded coordinates.

insights.title: Fire remarks appear only in July and August
insights.essence: All 61 ALA remarks naming fire fall in July (27) and August (27) plus January (7); every other month records zero.
insights.detail: Vehicle strike remarks are spread more evenly but peak in August (28), October (24) and November (23), while the biggest remark months are October (726), November (692) and December (637). The fire pattern is a sharp clustering that could reflect hazard-reduction burn season recording rather than year-round fire exposure. Checking the underlying remark text against burn schedules would confirm which it is.
insights.caveat: Monthly counts track survey and reporting effort as much as events; remark volume more than quintuples from May (92) to October (726), so month-to-month differences cannot be read as changes in how often koalas were harmed.

insights.title: Harvest is complete but georeferencing metadata is absent
insights.essence: Both harvests reconciled fully (5,398 of 5,398 and 58 of 58 records, all valid), yet four georeferencing metadata flags fire on 100.0% of ALA records.
insights.detail: Missing georeference date, georeferenced-by, georeference sources and verification status each apply to every ALA record. That means you cannot tell who placed a coordinate, when, from what source, or whether anyone checked it. The counts themselves are trustworthy; the provenance of the positions is not documented.
insights.caveat: Missing metadata fields do not mean the coordinates themselves are wrong; BioNet's median uncertainty of 50 m suggests many are precise.

limitations: Counts reflect who was out looking and writing notes, not how many koalas there are; nothing here supports a statement about population or trend.
All text figures come from the keyword baseline, which is approximate regular expressions; no model classifier results are in the pack.
The pack has no spatial breakdown below state level, so it cannot point to particular roads, suburbs or local government areas.
One year of data with no earlier or later window means no comparison over time is possible.
nextQuestions: Would a model classifier confirm the 15.0% harm share and the disease-over-vehicle-strike ordering that the keyword baseline reports?
Why are 9 openly licensed iNaturalist sightings absent from ALA, and is the shortfall a one-off or a standing pipeline gap?
Where in NSW do the 181 vehicle strike and 355 disease remarks fall, so mitigation can be targeted?
